items.title: Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models
Published
November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 39
+33 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow
Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!
Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.
In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.
This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.
Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.
Table of Contents
Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors
Token Pooling
Choosing a Pooling Budget
Calibrating Adaptive Pooling
Token Pooling-Aware Training
A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers
Optional Kernel Acceleration
Using the Trained Model
Evaluation Results
Combining Compression Techniques
References
Code and Models
Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors
A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.
For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:
MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d
\operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d
MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d
Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.
The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.
Token Pooling
HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.
These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.
You can make compression proportional to document length:
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.
Choosing a Pooling Budget
HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:
Setting
What it expresses
max_tokens=16
A maximum of 16 vectors per document, including protected tokens.
pool_factor=4
Approximately one quarter of each document's original vectors.
distance_threshold=...
A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry.
This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.
Calibrating Adaptive Pooling
Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.
Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
model = MultiVectorEncoder("lightonai/LateOn")
calibration_embeddings = model.encode_document(calibration_documents)
threshold = HierarchicalTokenPooling.calibrate_distance_threshold(calibration_embeddings, target_tokens=16)
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(distance_threshold=threshold)
# Apply pooling, targeting an average of 16 vectors per document
document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents_to_index, token_pooling=pooling)
Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.
Token Pooling-Aware Training
Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.
If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.
For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:
Retrieval using the original document embeddings.
Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors.
I average them:
L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled
\mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}}
L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​
The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.
Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.
A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.losses import (
CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss,
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss,
)
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
model = MultiVectorEncoder("answerdotai/ModernBERT-base", similarity_fn_name="maxsim")
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
base_loss = CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, mini_batch_size=64)
loss = MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss(
model,
base_loss,
token_poolings=[None, pooling],
weights=[0.5, 0.5],
)
CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.
Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.
The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.
Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.
The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:
uv run examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py --baseline
uv run examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py
The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.
You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:
pip install -U huggingface_hub
hf auth login
hf jobs uv run \
--flavor a10g-small \
--timeout 4h \
--secrets HF_TOKEN \
-- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/main/examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py
This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.
Optional Kernel Acceleration
You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:
pip install -U "sentence-transformers[train,kernels]"
In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:
model = MultiVectorEncoder(
"answerdotai/ModernBERT-base",
device="cuda",
similarity_fn_name="maxsim",
use_kernels=True,
)
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.
Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.
The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.
Using the Trained Model
Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
model = MultiVectorEncoder("tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-token-pooling")
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
queries = ["Which planet is known as the Red Planet?"]
documents = [
"Venus is often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and proximity.",
"Mars, known for its reddish appearance, is often referred to as the Red Planet.",
"Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, has a prominent red spot.",
]
query_embeddings = model.encode_query(queries)
document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents, token_pooling=pooling)
print([len(embedding) for embedding in document_embeddings])
# [5, 6, 5]
print(model.similarity(query_embeddings, document_embeddings))
# tensor([[16.0037, 25.9879, 22.8159]], device='cuda:0')
# For comparison, the same model without token pooling:
# [18, 21, 19]
# tensor([[16.6115, 27.6060, 24.1766]], device='cuda:0')
The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.
You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).
Evaluation Results
To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:
tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-token-pooling-baseline, using only the cached contrastive loss.
tomaarsen/mve-ModernBERT-base-token-pooling, using the cached contrastive loss wrapped with the unpooled and factor-4 objectives above.
Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.
I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.
At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.
The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.
Combining Compression Techniques
If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:
Embedding quantization to 4, 2, or 1 bit(s), for example via Fast-PLAID, to reduce storage per coordinate.
Token pooling to reduce the number of document vectors, optionally with pooling-aware fine-tuning as shown in this blog.
Matryoshka token embeddings to reduce the dimensionality of each token vector, optionally with fine-tuning to preserve retrieval quality at smaller widths.
If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.
MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.
Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.
With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

items.summary: 左文雯 张哲旸 2026-11-11 10:36 浙江 把业务规则变成AI可读、可追溯的结构化知识。为AI SQL Coding提供精确输入。 AI 写 SQL，快不等于能交付。在阿里的业务体系中，一个经营分析需求往往要关联数十甚至上百张表，同名字段在不同场景下含义不同，指标口径还会随业务迭代不断变化。更棘手的是，大量业务规则从没写进文档，只存在于历史生产代码和资深研发的经验里。新人要花几个月才能上手，团队的经验也很难复制。由于缺少对业务知识的了解，当大模型开始帮忙写 SQL时，这个问题就变得突出。 为此，我们引入本体（Ontology），从生产代码中自动抽取隐性的业务规则，把它们变成 AI 可读、可追溯的结构化知识。为 AI SQL Coding 提供精确输入。 AI 生成 SQL 的三类典型错误 当大模型作为辅助开发工具进入数据开发场景，矛盾变得突出：模型的代码生成速度远超人类，但做出正确判断所需的业务知识，它无从获取。 ▐1.1 一个看似简单的需求 以一个常见需求为例：业务方说「帮我查一下上月各品类的 top 品牌成交额及同比数据。」 需求只有一句话，看上去也不复杂。通用大模型几秒就能生成一段语法完整的 SQL，SELECT、FROM、WHERE、GROUP BY 结构齐全，逻辑通顺。但对照需求细看，问题就会暴露：品类下的品牌数据该从哪张表取？成交额对应哪个字段、是否包含退款？同比的口径又是什么？ 这些判断在 SQL 里没有标准答案。研发凭经验秒懂，模型只能猜。 ▐1.2 三类高频错误 真实开发中上述问题很常见，我们把通用 AI 的生成错误归纳为三类： 选错表。同一数据域下常有明细表、汇总表、快照表等十余张相似表，粒度各不相同。AI 分不清这些表之间的区别，容易选一张看着对实则不满足需求的表。 用错字段。同名字段在不同表中含义不同，同一含义在不同表中对应的字段名也不同。AI 直接按关键词匹配字段名，很可能选中与需求不符的字段。 口径对不上。指标计算往往有一套约定俗成的口径：分子分母各取什么、是否剔除特殊数据、时间窗口怎么定义。成交额是实付金额还是剔退款金额？这些约定通常不在需求文档里，而在历史代码和个人经验中。 ▐1.3 共同特征：SQL 能跑，数据不对 这三类错误有一个共同特征：SQL 能正常执行、能返回结果、不报任何错，但数据就是不对。这也意味着它们无法被常规测试拦截：没有异常、没有报错，只有错误的数据流进看板。本质：AI 缺的不是语法能力，是做出正确判断所需的业务知识。 下一章拆解这个「业务知识」具体缺在哪。 根因分析：AI 的知识缺口 在谈解法之前，先要看清AI生成SQL时，缺的业务知识到底是什么？拿两个需求拆开看。…

items.summary: 视频架构 2026-11-11 18:00 北京 AI MediaKit Skill 发布以来，我们陆续收到了许多开发者用户的投稿，他们结合真实使用场景，分享了自己从接入到成片的体验和测试记录。我们从中精选了几篇，陆续与大家分享。 ⚠️文中测试结论以及价格、耗时、效果等数据，主要基于作者在特定素材、测试方法和实际环境下的实测结果，具体表现请以实际产品页面、公示价格、账单及使用场景为准。 作者：CSDN 几何心凉 本文为节选转载，内容仅代表作者个人观点；全文可点击【阅读原文】阅读。 一、引言：为什么要把视频处理交给 Agent 视频后处理里有大量“知道该做什么、但不想自己动手”的环节：老素材分辨率不够要增强，搬运或二创素材带着硬字幕要擦除，一小时的长视频要剪出能用的片段。这些活拆开看都不难，但串起来就是一下午的重复劳动——开剪辑软件、导素材、调参数、等导出、再导下一个。 大模型 Agent 擅长理解自然语言指令，但让它直接“处理视频”一直隔着一层：模型本身不碰音视频，得有手有脚的工具。MCP 和 Agent Skill 解决的就是这层连接问题。火山引擎视频云最近把自家的智能媒体处理能力打包成了 AI MediaKit Skill——一套可以被 Trae、Cursor、Claude Code 这类 Agent 直接调用的技能包，号称覆盖 80 项音视频与图像处理能力。 我关心的问题很实际：它对 Agent 是不是真的“开箱即用”？增强、擦除、剪辑这三件核心的事，效果到底到什么水平？长任务跑起来是什么体验？按量计费会不会一不小心超预算？这篇文章就围绕这三个方向，把安装配置、单项实测、组合流水线完整跑一遍，给出带数据的结论。 二、产品概览与核心能力 AI MediaKit Skill 的载体是火山引擎开源的命令行工具 mediakit-cli：技能包装进 Agent 后，Agent 通过自然语言理解需求，再调用 CLI 完成实际处理。不过我们也可以通过豆包工作这类agent工具来直接调用我们的AI MediaKit Skill。整个能力集按对象拆成 5 个技能包： 图1 AI MediaKit Skill 能力版图：5 个技能包、80 项原子能力 几个值得注意的结构性设计： 第一，本地与云端双模。 裁剪、拼接、转场这类确定性操作走本地 FFmpeg（秒级完成、不产生费用）；画质增强、字幕擦除、语义切片这类 AI 能力走云端任务。Agent 会按能力性质自动选路，也可以用 --local / --cloud 强制指定。 第二，异步任务模型统一。 云端 AI 能力全部是“提交任务 → 返回 task_id → shared query-task 轮询 → 拿到结果地址”的闭环。长任务不会阻塞会话，Agent 可以在等待期间先汇报阶段性状态，这一点对“把活交给…

items.title: 来 SEE Conf 看懂 Personal Agent 的能力边界与落地路径！
items.summary: 原创 SEE Conf 组委会 2026-11-11 08:26 浙江 早鸟票将于今天截止！ SEE Conf 2026 将于 11 月 28 日在杭州举办。早鸟票将于明天（11 月 12 日）23:59:59 截止，抢票地址：https://seeconf.antgroup.com 蚂蚁集团灵光产品经理 杨诚（漠念） 将在「AI 创新体验」专题给大家带来主题为《从工具到伙伴 - 蚂蚁灵光的 AI Agent 实践》的演讲。 浙江大学 APRIL 实验室博士生刘广义 将在 「卓越 AI 工程实践」专题给大家带来主题为《nanoMuse: Personal Agent 的系统架构与算法实践》的演讲。 当 AI 从“工具”走向“伙伴”，一个新物种正在悄然改变我们与数字世界的关系 —— Personal Agent。 它不是又一个聊天机器人，而是一个真正“懂你”的存在：记住你的习惯，理解你的意图，在恰当的时机主动为你完成任务。 这背后既是产品哲学的转向 —— 从“人找服务”到“服务找人”，也是技术栈的跃迁——从单轮对话走向长记忆、多模态、工具调用与自主规划的智能体架构。 杨诚（漠念）将从产品视角聊 Personal Agent 如何重新定义人机协作的体验边界。 刘广义将以 nanoMuse 为例从技术视角拆解其系统架构与核心算法。 两条线交汇之处，共同勾勒出现阶段 Personal Agent 在终端层面的落地图景。 「AI 创新体验」专题介绍 AI 的价值不止于技术突破，更在于打开新的体验可能。 本专题聚焦 AI 如何让人突破专业、成本与协作的门槛，把构想变成可感知的作品与服务。从多模态生成式界面、跨端协同到具身交互，探讨智能如何进入日常、成为你能用得上的能力；从 Personal Agent、人机协同到群体智能，看智能如何拓展个人与团队的创造边界。汇聚一线产品与工程团队，分享从原型到真实产品的落地经验，让创造的增量转化为你我真实可感的体验价值。 「卓越 AI 工程实践」专题介绍 本专题共设置 8 个演讲主题，聚焦一线落地的真实挑战，避开纸面理论，深入探讨研发范式重塑、复杂 Agent 系统架构与线上 Badcase 稳定性治理。 从工具链革新到客户端工程落地，分享来自蚂蚁、阿里、字节及高校团队的专家经验，解析如何用工程手段让 AI 跑通业务闭环，帮助从业者把 AI 从 Demo 原型推向高质量上线，真正跑起来、用起来、产生价值。 点击下方小程序抢早鸟票！ 让我们一起相约 SEE Conf 2026， 创造力复兴，从你我开始。 11 月 28 日，我们不见不散！ 阅读原文 跳转微信打开

items.title: AI从Working、Coding到Oncall：腾讯视频如何让知识流动起来？
items.summary: 原创 腾讯程序员 2026-11-10 17:36 广东 让知识流动起来：视频技术部 AI 原生知识沉淀的实践与思考 作者：adawswang 共同作者：seasonzhou 我们常调侃自己讨厌两类人，一类是不写文档的人，另一类是让我写文档的人。文档是知识的一种，在AI生产力爆炸的今天，有了 AI 似乎就能轻松建知识库、快速写文档，好像「既要又要」唾手可得。但是真的是这样吗？ 在视频这个复杂业务体系下，我们有 Working、Coding、OnCall 三类常见的典型工作，分别对应业务、交付、运维支撑业务——知识是它们共同的底座，本文我们将来分享视频技术部在知识方面的一些思考和实践。 一、背景：从个人到组织提效的转变1.1 知识：组织型 AI 的土壤 烟火盛宴 · 个人型 AI 的狂欢：上半年是一个“个人型AI的盛大狂欢”，人人都成了“全栈”、个人效率看似数以十倍在疯涨、个人想法也以指数级在喷涌而出，看起来个人的效率已经快到了难以置信的程度，“一个人能xxx / 几分钟能xxx……”，诸如此类的宣传不绝于耳，然而从组织视角来看，组织的效率、组织的有效产出/进展却远远没有这种体感。 烟花易冷 · 个人的火如何照亮组织：为什么会有这样的现象产生？核心问题在于：个人效率↑ ≠ 组织产出↑，个人技能提升了，但是组织的工作流并没有得到重塑。我们从过去的历史进程中学习到，伴随着每一次工业革命，可观测到的生产率在短期内不仅没有增长，反而出现停滞甚至下降的经济现象，身处AI时代的今天，我们面临了同样问题，这些问题集中体现在： 知识不沉淀：最好的 prompt、经验、上下文锁在个人脑里/本地，离职即蒸发。 能力不复用：A 的最佳实践无法自动传给 B，组织在"重复造火花"。 标准不统一：人人 Vibe Coding，质量参差，治理失控。 上下文孤岛：AI 拿不到组织级的数据 / 血缘 / 规范，只能在个人范围打转。 AI 鸿沟：用得好和用不好的人差距被拉大，组织被撕裂而并非被抬升。 企业特性缺失：缺乏权限管控、审计日志、合规审查等企业级必备能力 流程失连：组织的工作是复杂的，通常是分散在各种零散的N多个系统上，系统内的技术债、经验债缺少治理/沉淀，系统间缺少衔接，协作难度高。 …… 经过上半年的摸索和实践，我们认为AI Agent在业务各场景的应用过程中是存在一个渐进式发展的路径的，我们基本形成了比较清晰的共识，建立了《L0～L5 的AI应用成熟度》模型，如下： 段位 名称 类比 人的角色 AI形态 L0 纯人工模式 无自动化 全部执行者 无 L1 AI工具渗透 驾驶辅助 工具使用者 独立AI应用 L2 AI流程嵌入 部分自动化 流程主导者 嵌入式Copilot L3 Agent协作 有条件自动化 审批者/决策者 Agent工作台 L4 高度自治 高度自动化 监督者/战略家…

items.title: Boxes
items.summary: Today, we're introducing something new to Amp: boxes. A box is an always-on computer to which you can deploy the many delightful things you've built with Amp. Boxes are small and cheap (the smallest one is $18 per 30 days). But they're full-on computers. You can run anything you want on them. They come with an agent running on them, too. And agents are great at running on computers. Today, with hyper-individual software being created nearly as fast as someone can dictate a prompt, a small machine goes a long way and can serve most personal or internal software. Software that you build for yourself and people you work with doesn't need to scale to thousands of users. All it needs to be is available for everyone you want to share with and within reach of an agent. That's what boxes are: a home for what you build with your agents. items.title: Cursor Projects is now multiplayer
items.summary:
Blog / productNov 10, 2026·product
Cursor Projects is now multiplayerAryaman Khandelwal · 4 min read
In September we introduced Projects, a way for engineers to take on large-scale work by directing a fleet of agents through a single coordinator. Today Projects gets a major upgrade: it's now multiplayer. Invite your teammates into a Project, and you can plan, build and ship together, alongside all of your agents. Multi-agent systems have so far served one person. Projects is a multi-agent system built for a whole team.
#A multiplayer, multi-agent workspace
Cursor ProjectsTeammatesEngineerDesignerPMCoordinatorsCoordinatorCoordinatorCoordinatorAgentsShared contextPlansDocsDesignsTasksSkillsMemories
Cursor ProjectsTeammatesEngineerDesignerPMCoordinatorsCoordinatorCoordinatorCoordinatorAgentsShared contextPlansDocsDesignsTasksSkillsMemories
Cursor ProjectsTeammatesEngineerDesignerPMCoordinatorsCoordinatorCoordinatorCoordinatorAgentsShared contextPlansDocsDesignsTasksSkillsMemories
There's no shortage of software for team collaboration, but ironically, none for coding agents. Projects is the first workspace where software teams work side by side with all of their agents, with shared context, memory, and documents. A shared task board shows who's doing what, what everyone's agents are working on, and the PR behind each task, giving humans and agents alike a unified, up-to-date view.
#A unified context system for a whole team
Today, agent context is siloed per person, and new team members have to build and maintain context before putting agents to work. In a Project, each teammate still gets their own one-to-one chat with their coordinator and worker agents, each with its own local context. On top of that, Projects adds a shared context system that holds requirements docs, diagrams, tech specs, mockups, and more. The shared layer is built once and grows with the team's work. A decision made in one chat is accessible to every agent in the Project. When a new teammate is invited to a Project, context is pre-configured and up to date, avoiding repetitive setup.
We've seen this most clearly in on-call. Several of our teams now run their on-call rotations in a shared Project. When one of our engineers recently took over the rotation from a teammate, their coordinator picked up right where things stood, after checking in first. It already knew what work was in flight, which issues were still unattended, which incidents and notes needed handing off, and which channels, Linear boards and threads to keep an eye on. In-progress work can even be handed over directly: the new person's agent simply takes it on.
#Agent-to-agent communication across teammates
A shared workspace and shared context open up agent-to-agent communication between teammates. This lets teammates' agents plan around and unblock each other in real time, just as people do.
For example, if an engineer is adding reviews to the product page while a designer is redesigning it, their coordinators spot the overlap early and sync up, so the reviews are built straight into the new design, with no refactors down the road. Or if your feature reads from a database while your teammate is changing the schema, your agents agree on the order of work up front, so neither of you hits a merge conflict at the end.
#Get Started
Multiplayer Projects brings the spirit of collaboration software to AI agents for the first time, giving human teams and agent fleets one shared space to work together. It's rolling out in beta to all users in Cursor starting today. To get started, create a Project from the left-hand nav, then invite your teammates to join.

items.title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Decision Models in Hugging Face
Published
November 10, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 109
+103 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow
Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0
> We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.", which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON.
[Start thinking]
...
[end thinking]
```json
{
"team_to_handle": "Billing",
"urgency": "High",
"request_refund": true
}
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'department': {
# 'type': 'choice',
# 'choice': 'billing',
# 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
# 'probabilities': {
# 'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
# 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
# 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
# }
# }
# }
This is the key idea behind decision models.
What are decision models?
A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)
For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:
State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities
Why not use LLMs for everything?
We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
However, there are a few problems with this approach.
LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.
How are decision models different from classification models?
Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.
Traditional classification
Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:
Billing
Technical support
Sales
A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.
The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.
If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.
Zero-shot classification
Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.
For example:
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
"zero-shot-classification",
model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
"My payment was deducted twice.",
candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
# 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'],
# 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]}
Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
"zero-shot-classification",
model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
"My payment was deducted twice.",
candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales", "legal"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
# 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'],
# 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]}
One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.
This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.
Where decision models differ
Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).
More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.
Consider these three approaches:
Property
Classification
Zero-shot classification
Decision model
Probability over choices
Yes
Yes
Yes
Labels defined at inference
No
Yes
Yes
Multiple typed questions
No
No
Yes
Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions
Task-specific
Possible with adaptation
Native primitives
The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.
The decision model interface
A decision model request has the following two components:
state
questions
State
The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.
For example:
{
"customer_message": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
"subscription": "pro",
"previous_tickets": 2
}
Questions and their primitives
Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:
Choice: Select one of several possible answers.
Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale.
Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically.
Let's go over them one by one.
Choice: A probability distribution over options
Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.
Suppose we ask:
Which department should handle this customer request?
The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'department': {
# 'type': 'choice',
# 'choice': 'billing',
# 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
# 'probabilities': {
# 'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
# 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
# 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
# }
# }
# }
The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:
pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj)
p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)}
pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​
Here, KKK is the number of choices.
Consider this illustrative distribution:
Choice
Probability
Billing
0.998
Technical support
0.001
Sales
0.001
The probabilities sum to one:
∑i=1Kpi=1.
\sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1.
i=1∑K​pi​=1.
The model chooses the option with the largest probability:
y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi
\hat y=\arg\max_i p_i
y^​=argimax​pi​
In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.
Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution
Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?
Consider the question:
How urgent is this customer request?
We define three levels:
0: Low urgency
1: Medium urgency
2: High urgency
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"urgency": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
"criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'urgency': {
# 'type': 'score',
# 'score': 1.7053890228271484,
# 'legend': {
# '0': 'low',
# '1': 'medium',
# '2': 'high'
# },
# 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814,
# 'probabilities': {
# '0': 0.014908230863511562,
# '1': 0.26479458808898926,
# '2': 0.7202972173690796
# }
# }
# }
The model again produces a probability distribution:
Level
Probability
0 — Low
0.01
1 — Medium
0.26
2 — High
0.72
Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.
For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:
E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i
E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​
For our example:
E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7
\mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7
E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7
The reported score is therefore 1.7.
This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.
Noul: A Bernoulli decision
The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.
For example:
Is the customer requesting a refund?
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"refund": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
}
}
}
)
# {
# 'refund': {
# 'type': 'noul',
# 'noul': 0.9947046637535095
# }
# }
Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).
Let YYY represent a binary outcome:
Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p)
Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)
Y∼Bernoulli(p)
where
P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.
P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p.
P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.
If the model returns:
{"type": "noul", "noul": 0.92}
it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.
The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.
Confidence: How certain is the model?
So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.
The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.
For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:
pmax⁡−1K1−1K
\frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}}
1−K1​pmax​−K1​​
where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.
The intuition here is:
A uniform distribution has confidence 0. pmax⁡=1Kp_{\max} = \frac{1}{K}pmax​=K1​. This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely.
A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. pmax⁡=1p_{\max} = 1pmax​=1
The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence.
In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:
C=3(0.998)−12=0.997
C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997
C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997
Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.
Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem
Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.
Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:
inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API
the Hub can package and surface them consistently
and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures
The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.
1. Serving with Transformers
Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
print(decide)
# DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'}
One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:
from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig
model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide"
config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id)
Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.
We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:
pip install "transformers[serving]"
transformers serve
Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"model": "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide",
"state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
"urgency": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
"criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
},
"refund": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
}
}
}'
The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.
{
"model":"autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide",
"answers":{
"department":{
"type":"choice",
"choice":"billing",
"confidence":0.9974000453948975,
"probabilities":{
"billing":0.9982666969299316,
"technical":0.0010246571619063616,
"sales":0.0007087149424478412
}
},
"urgency":{
"type":"score",
"score":1.7525686174631119,
"legend":{"0":"low","1":"medium","2":"high"},
"confidence":0.6288529792800546,
"probabilities":{
"0":0.014000383205711842,
"1":0.2194305807352066,
"2":0.7665690183639526
}
},
"refund":{
"type":"noul",
"noul":0.9953224062919617
}
},
"usage":{"input_tokens":148,"output_tokens":0}
}
An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.
2. Serving with llama.cpp
llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.
For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF
The default server runs on port 9931.
We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.
The useful property is interface compatibility.
curl http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF",
"state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
"urgency": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
"criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
},
"refund": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
}
}
}'
3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub
Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.
For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.
4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling
Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.
Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:
each example is a decision request (a state plus questions) paired with the gold answer.
model.decision_config.prepare_inputs turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time.
the model returns one logit per option, so a choice question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options.
import os; os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"]="2"
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments
checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
examples = [
("I was charged twice. Please refund me.", "refund"),
("My package has not arrived.", "shipping"),
("The application crashes when I open it.", "technical"),
("I want my money back.", "refund"),
("Where is my delivery?", "shipping"),
("I cannot log into my account.", "technical"),
]
options = {
"refund": "Billing issues and refunds",
"shipping": "Orders and deliveries",
"technical": "Software and account issues",
}
def preprocess(text, label):
request = {
"state": text,
"questions": {
"category": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Classify the support request.",
"criteria": options,
}
},
}
(inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs(
request, tokenizer
)
inputs["marks"] = inputs["marks"].unsqueeze(0)
inputs["num_options"] = torch.tensor([[len(questions[0].options)]])
inputs["question_type_ids"] = torch.tensor([[1]]) # choice
inputs["labels"] = torch.tensor(
[questions[0].options.index(label)]
)
return inputs
dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples]
class DecisionTrainer(Trainer):
def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, **kwargs):
inputs = inputs.copy()
labels = inputs.pop("labels")
logits = model(**inputs)
logits = logits.unsqueeze(0) # [3] -> [1, 3]
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.float(), labels)
return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss
trainer = DecisionTrainer(
model=model,
args=TrainingArguments(
output_dir="./decision-toy",
max_steps=30,
per_device_train_batch_size=1,
learning_rate=1e-3,
logging_steps=5,
save_strategy="no",
report_to="none",
remove_unused_columns=False,
),
train_dataset=dataset,
data_collator=lambda batch: batch[0],
)
trainer.train()
First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.
If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.
Final thoughts
Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.
Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.
Community ashhadahsan 11 days ago
Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.
I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.
Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator
For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Gemini 4 Carbon and /swarmThe Antigravity Team·Nov 10, 2026·3 min readShareCopy linkShare on XShare on BlueskyShare on LinkedInShare
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Carbon inside Google Antigravity alongside /swarm (in preview), pairing our strongest model for long-horizon software engineering, knowledge work, scientific discovery, and cybersecurity with native multi-agent team orchestration.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon to work with /swarm
Working with a single agent works well for scoped tasks, but breaks down when a change spans dozens of files and test suites. Dynamic subagents evolved that into a primary agent spinning off isolated helper agents: powerful for delegating one-off tasks, but still bottlenecked by a single coordinator context reviewing, synthesizing, and routing every step. With /swarm, working with Antigravity turns into orchestrating a coordinated system of specialized agents that plan, build, and verify in parallel.
Instead of brittle hierarchical chains where context degrades, /swarm passes your prompt to a family of agents: a coordinator that spins up specialized parallel workers in isolated git worktrees so edits never collide, and adversarial verifiers dedicated to running tests and challenging diffs. Every agent collaborates directly on a shared, append-only message board, parking at zero token cost when idle and activating the instant an agent needs input.
Typing /swarm in the composer as the coordinator spins up parallel workers and a verifier that post to the shared message board.
To keep multi-agent execution transparent rather than an opaque black box, /swarm ships with a built-in Swarm UI in Antigravity’s side pane (and a live full-screen terminal board via /swarm board or Alt+S in the CLI):
Live Board, Roster, and Graph replay: Watch your agent team debate trade-offs in real time on the Board feed, inspect live tool activity or jump into any agent’s trajectory from the Members roster to steer it, and scrub through the interactive Graph timeline to see how the team converged from initial brief to verified code.
Clicking through the Board feed, Members roster, and interactive Graph timeline in the Swarm side pane.
Right-sized multi-model teams with Gemini 4 Carbon: Because agents in a swarm can be pinned to different models, you can match model intelligence to each role. While Gemini 4 Argon remains an ideal choice for most advanced engineering and knowledge work tasks, Carbon is built to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops using more tokens (ranking #1 on CursorBench 4.0 and Perplexity’s WANDR). That makes Carbon ideal for high-leverage coordinator, architecture, cybersecurity auditing, and adversarial verification roles while lighter, faster models handle the parallel file edits and routine implementation tasks.
Pinning an agent to Gemini 4 Carbon from the Members roster, alongside workers running on Gemini 4 Argon.
Inside Google, in five weeks of internal dogfooding of /swarm, Google engineers ran swarms to tackle gnarly multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. (As a fair warning, even with zero-token idle waits and dynamic model hot-swapping, parallel multi-agent systems consume quota much faster than a standard chat.)
Getting started
When your ambition outgrows a single conversation, /swarm with Gemini 4 Carbon puts an entire multi-agent team behind your keyboard. Starting today, Google AI Ultra subscribers can build with Gemini 4 Carbon in the Antigravity App, the Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity IDE extensions, and /swarm is rolling out today in preview across the Antigravity App and CLI. Enterprises can access Gemini 4 Carbon in Gemini for business, and scientists and researchers can apply for a chance to get access to both Argon and Carbon via Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months.

items.summary: An application can have an authentication check and still expose data if a caller can bypass the service that enforces it. When the services and deployment settings live in separate repositories, spotting that gap requires examining how they work together. In a microservices application, the API gateway and orders service might live in separate repositories. The gateway checks a user's token and passes their ID to the orders service, which uses it to return that user's orders. If a caller can reach the orders service directly, they could send someone else's ID and access their orders. items.title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
Published
November 10, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 13
+7 Zaïd Alhadad zaid-alhadad Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michelle Habonneau michellehbn Follow
You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.
Why pay through Google Cloud?
Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.
If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:
One bill: your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend.
No new vendor to onboard: purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process.
Everything is covered: upgrading your org to a Team or Enterprise subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at public Hugging Face pricing.
If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.
1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace
Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".
You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".
Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.
2. Link your Hugging Face organization
You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.
You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.
Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.
3. Subscription approved
Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.
To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.
Congratulations!
Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.
A few things worth knowing:
Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace.
Included credits still apply: if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud.
Monitor your usage at any time from the billing section of your organization settings, and find the charges in the Billing reports of the Google Cloud console.
Linking and unlinking are audited: both actions are recorded in your organization's audit logs.
Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

items.title: 从淘小蜜分流模型的实践，聊聊 Jev 与 System One
items.summary: 原创 吴双 2026-11-10 18:01 浙江 关于最近大火的 Jev，本文或许能够提供一些技术实践参考 这是2026年的第 79 篇文章 （ 本文阅读时间：约 30 分钟 ） 前言 最近 Jev 很火，技术社区里也出现了不少复现项目。看完相关文档和项目后，我发现团队去年做的淘小蜜客服 Agent 分流模型和 Jev 要解决的问题有一些相似之处，技术方案上也存在可以互相验证的地方。 本文的初稿其实在去年九月份就已经写好了，当时的内容主要是总结淘小蜜分流模型的数据构建、训练和部署经验；最近分流模型又做了一轮优化，在线上部署和评测时踩了四五天坑，再加上 Jev 发布后大家都在猜它的实现方式，所以重新把之前的内容整理了一番。 先说明，Jev 没有公开模型结构和具体训练方法。本文对 Jev 的介绍以 TypeSafe 官方文档为准，对模型结构的讨论主要参考 SemIf、open-bonsai-jev、AlexWortega/openjev 等社区项目；社区项目只能说明某种方案可以实现类似能力，不能说明 Jev 内部一定采用了相同方案。 01 背景 淘小蜜客服 Agent 在回答用户问题前需要先判断应由哪个 Agent 承接，当前的分流模型主要把用户问题分成售前、售后、其他问题、意图不清四类，再根据分类结果路由到不同的 Agent。 这个任务表面上是一个普通四分类，实际做起来却没有那么简单。售前和售后的标准不是按照通用语义划分，而是按照不同 Agent 的能力边界划分。例如订单评价、取消订单、价保、退款后的优惠券和红包等问题属于售前。“退差价”也不能见词就判：因质量不符、重量不足、少件、描述不符等商家责任要求退差价，属于售后；没有这些商家责任原因的退差价，属于售前。猫超、国际、百补、小时达、闪购等自营场景的问题，如果超出当前 Agent 的承接范围，又可能归为其他问题。这些规则带有较强的业务属性，和通用大模型在预训练阶段学到的常识并不完全一致。 在分流模型的迭代过程中，主要经历三个阶段。 第一阶段是使用通用 LLM 做 ICL few-shot 分类。 具体做法是在 prompt 中描述分类规则，再放入一些示例，让模型直接输出分类标签。这种方案开发比较快，前期效果也能满足基本需求，但是存在几个问题： 大模型调用成本较高，响应速度较慢，大促高峰期还有系统稳定性的问题。 业务规则和通用常识冲突时，仅调整 prompt 很难完全纠正模型。 对于退款权益、红包、退差价等边界 case，继续增加 few-shot 的收益逐渐变小。 第二阶段是对 7B 模型做 SFT。 这一阶段用约 2.1 万条数据做 SFT，把业务知识教给 7B…

items.title: 快手电商智能补贴实践：从经验发券走向目标驱动的智能营销托管
items.summary: 快手技术 2026-11-10 18:10 北京 从“发券”到“经营”：快手电商如何让补贴带来真实增量。 每次电商大促启动前，运营团队都需要回答一连串具体问题：预算怎样分配，消费券发给谁，门槛和面额怎样设置，什么时候放量，效果不及预期时又该调整哪里？ 这些问题看似分散，背后指向的是同一个经营目标：在预算和钱效约束下，让补贴带来更多真实增量。 回看快手电商这几年的营销技术建设，营销补贴的重点也在持续演进：从支撑活动快速上线和大规模覆盖，到基于人群与场景的精细化运营，再到围绕经营目标开展增量预估、预算优化与智能决策，并逐步推进营销托管。 一、从人工经验发券到智能决策：为什么“发得多”不等于“长得好” 1.1 粗放式营销：先把活动感知打出去 先看一组数据：2023年年货节大促，10天活动时间，累计发放优惠券数十亿张，触达近亿用户，平均每位用户发放数十张优惠券。这个数字能够体现当时的券投放规模，统一券包、统一门槛、集中投放，可以快速把活动推起来，让用户感知到平台在做大促。对技术团队来说，这个阶段的重点是把券配置、券发放和券核销链路做好，支撑大规模投放。 在业务早期，运营制定一套规则，系统将优惠券发给用户，发券量、领取率和核销率成为最容易观察的指标。随着业务规模扩大，更关键的是判断：这些优惠券究竟带来了多少额外购买？哪些用户原本就会下单，哪些用户需要优惠才能促成购买，又有哪些用户即使获得优惠也不会购买？同一张券作用于不同用户，产生的增量可能相差很大，需要进一步区分自然转化与补贴带来的真实增量，如下图的营销四象限所示： 营销敏感：不发券时则不买，发了优惠券则购买 自然转化：不论是否发优惠券均会购买 无动于衷: 不论是否发优惠券均不会购买 反作用： 不发优惠券会购买，发了优惠券反而不买 这一阶段主要解决了营销活动的用户覆盖问题，但对于哪些营销投入真正促成了增量购买，仍缺乏清晰的判断。 1.2 精细化营销：让不同人群匹配不同策略，也让复杂度快速上升 随着用户标签、场景识别和营销配置能力逐步完善，我们开始围绕人群与场景制定差异化策略：针对新客、回流用户和活跃用户采用不同的补贴方式，结合直播间、短视频和商城的消费路径，以及用户的类目偏好、消费能力和价格敏感度，调整触达方式、券门槛和面额。这一步将运营经验沉淀为系统可执行的规则，也通过策略配置、实验验证和效果复盘，为后续智能化积累了数据与执行能力。 但“人群 × 场域 × 券档 × 时间段”的组合不断扩大，策略之间可能交叉，同一人群内部也存在需求差异，人工调整难以持续跟上大促期间流量、货盘和用户行为的变化。 差异化策略改善了发券效果，但策略的生产和迭代仍然高度依赖人工，专业壁垒和人力产能逐渐成为规模化的瓶颈：…

items.title: 美团 LongCat-2.5 正式开源：从看见，到抵达
items.summary: 美团正式开源 LongCat-2.5，采用 MIT 协议，支持商用推理部署与二次训练，无需额外授权。 LongCat-2.5是面向长程智能体任务的原生多模态模型，在复杂代码库开发、完整项目构建、Visual Coding 与专业办公场景中，端到端交付能力均有明显提升。模型总参数 1.6 万亿，每个 token 激活约 480 亿参数，支持一百万上下文。针对显存与带宽受限的国产算力芯片，我们在模型架构、芯片适配与部署策略上也进行了深度协同优化。 完整分数与评测条件参见技术博客 01 代码与长程智能体 LongCat-2.5 的长程能力提升，来自一整条训练链路的扩展，而非单点改动。这些设计不改变模型能力的定义，但让能力在长任务中稳定发挥。 第一，更贴近真实长程任务的训练数据。加入更多长程轨迹，并把真实 Agent 的失败轨迹转为可复现、可验证的训练任务。 第二，更适配长任务节奏的强化学习。采用partial rollout 异步训练，让未跑完的长任务保存后续跑；过采样率按通过率动态调整，过滤全对全错的样本组；对跨 checkpoint 的旧轨迹做梯度校正，降低陈旧偏差。 第三，更有效减少“钻空子”的训练约束。任务环境断网、清除 git 历史与文件缓存，以 LLM judge 监督轨迹；对重复思考、重复工具调用、过度思考施加约束，让模型专注完成任务。 | 查看开发者们的端到端测评示例，可帮助大家观察模型在真实使用流程中的表现。 02 Visual Coding 与 3D LongCat-2.5 在 Visual Coding 上表现出色，支持创意设计、3D 等任务。这些能力提升来自视觉表征层的改造：模型将视觉信号表示为多层级离散 token，与文本一样由主干模型统一处理，而非外挂视觉模块。具体而言，模型对原生分辨率视觉特征做残差向量量化，逐级补足细节；视觉 token 可离线预计算并缓存，减少在线计算量，也让分布式训练负载更均衡；视觉码本与主干联合训练，视觉与文本共享同一套主干参数，在同一语义空间内协同完成视觉理解与代码生成。 | 查看开发者们的端到端测评示例，可帮助大家观察模型在真实使用流程中的表现。 03 专业办公与商业分析 专业办公场景对模型的要求，不是单点问答，而是同时完成几件事：读得多份材料，抓得住关键信息，形成专业判断，并把判断转化为规范、可用的交付物。LongCat-2.5 在这个场景的提升也围绕这条链路展开：材料处理更稳，专业判断更贴近分析人员，报告、演示文稿和办公工具能够端到端交付，多轮任务执行更可靠。目标不是为每个场景单独建模，而是让主线模型具备端到端完成专业办公任务的能力。 支撑这些提升的，是一组相互配合的技术设计。多专家在线教学负责将领域能力融入主线模型：学生先自主作答，专家再通过全词表 KL…

items.title: AI and Irontown
items.summary: For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting. A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it. The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns. Google Antigravity for Knowledge WorkThe Antigravity Team·Nov 9, 2026·4 min readShareCopy linkShare on XShare on BlueskyShare on LinkedInShare
As the adoption of Google Antigravity has scaled, we’ve seen people bring Antigravity far more than code. Alongside software engineering, more and more daily sessions center on deep research, data analysis, drafting documents and presentations, prototyping designs, and automating everyday workflows. We’ve seen this exact same pull inside Google, where tens of thousands of Googlers outside software engineering (across sales, finance, legal, product, design, research, marketing, and operations) now rely on Antigravity every week alongside engineers to get their work done.
Software development at the core, built with every role in mind
We are in the business of helping the world deliver value through products and research. No matter what you are working on, the underlying logic and systems eventually need to be built, and that requires software development. That’s why software development is, and will remain, at the core of what Antigravity enables.
But actually delivering value never happens in a silo. It requires every role—engineering, product, design, data, science, operations, and go-to-market—working together with a common language, shared context, and mutual understanding. And the exact same agentic capabilities forged on complex software engineering (multi-step reasoning, working directly across local folders and connected tools, orchestrating subagents and plugins, and iterating on rich artifacts) are what make an agent genuinely useful for rigorous knowledge work, too.
Supporting knowledge work shouldn’t mean pointing non-developers to a watered-down experience, nor should it mean forcing everyone to navigate Git worktrees, terminal panes, and line-by-line code diffs just to collaborate with an agent. That’s why Antigravity is built with everyone doing knowledge work in mind, and why today we are launching a new Knowledge Work user experience in Google Antigravity to support both software engineering and broader knowledge work.
One Antigravity agent, tailored to how you work
While Antigravity’s default UI was built around repositories, terminals, and code diffs, you can now choose between two interface layouts in the Antigravity App: Knowledge Work and Software Engineering. Both layouts run the exact same Antigravity agent, with full access to frontier models, local files, plugins, skills, rules, custom agents, and MCP servers, so these visual changes make Antigravity more approachable and intuitive for professional knowledge work without giving up any underlying capability.
Alongside interface layouts, we’ve rolled out an updated role-based onboarding flow for new users. When signing in for the first time, you can select what best describes your work (starting with Software Engineering, Knowledge Work, Data & Analytics, Science, or Design) to automatically tailor your starting interface layout, starter prompts, and recommended plugins right out of the box.
How to switch
In Google Antigravity, open Settings > General > Interface Layout (Cmd+, on macOS or Ctrl+, on Windows and Linux).
Select Knowledge Work or Software Engineering (the default for existing users).
Switching takes effect immediately across open and new conversations with no restart needed.
Switching between Knowledge Work and Software Engineering in Google Antigravity.
What changes in the Knowledge Work layout
Streamlined projects & sidebar: Creates folder-backed projects and standalone No Project conversations directly without Git worktree prompts, and hides Git branch pickers and IDE handoff buttons.
Cleaner conversation thread & approvals: Replaces expandable tool-call groups, inline code diffs (+/- line counts), and subagent cards with a live progress line that clears once the turn finishes, keeps focus on replies and artifacts, and presents plain-language summaries on permission prompts.
Outputs-focused Overview & Side Panel: Stays tucked away until a conversation produces output, removes Review and Terminal, renames the Files tree to Folders, and centers on Documents, Artifacts, Links, Uploads, and Background Tasks (keeping Plugins when UI plugins or MCP Apps are active).
Simplified Customizations & Settings: Highlights installed Plugins in the Installed tab (while configured skills, rules, custom agents, and MCP servers continue running in the background) and tucks developer controls (Terminal, Workspaces, and detailed permission rules) under Advanced Settings.
Read the full breakdown in the documentation.
Just the start
While coding and software engineering remain the core of Antigravity and what we build, we can recognize when our users are pushing the platform in new ways, and we want to meet our users where they are. A tailored layout is just the beginning. Stay tuned for more updates that make Antigravity a safe, first-class platform for every kind of knowledge work.
Download Google Antigravity to try the new Knowledge Work layout today.

items.title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
Community Article Published
November 9, 2026 Upvote 14
+8 Atsunori Fujita Atsunori Follow nvidia Masaya Ogushi SnowMasaya Follow nvidia Vincent Gong vg1024 Follow nvidia Kotaro Yamamoto kyamamoto-nv Follow nvidia Yoshi Suhara suhara Follow nvidia Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).
This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.
What’s in the Dataset?
9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese
50 fields per record: 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics
~1.5B tokens total, including ~750M persona tokens
~950k unique names
1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce
Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes
Diverse persona types: Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns
Natural language persona attributes: Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning
Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license
How We Built It
Data Generation Pipeline
It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:
NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0): A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation
gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0): For Japanese text generation
Enhanced Cultural Context
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:
Education: Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways.
Occupation: We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training.
Life Stages: We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas.
Household Finances: In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds.
Digital & Financial Literacy: By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases.
Private By Design
Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people.
Who This Data Is For
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.
The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.
Practical AI Applications
The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:
Multi-turn conversation: Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets.
Domain-specific AI development: Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases.
Bias testing and fairness: Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society.
Why It Matters
Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.
Data Diversity: Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of model collapse.
Cultural Authenticity: Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of Sovereign AI systems.
Privacy and Governance: Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it.
By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk.
Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan
Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.
Start Building with Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan
You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language.
from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset("nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan")
Use cases for building production-ready applications:
Using personas as seeds for dialogue generation
Fine-tuning models with culturally grounded data
Building personalized engines that reflect Japan's overall demographic makeup
Developing domain-specific AI agents equipped with Japanese context
From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications.
